title: How Transcendentalism Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore Transcendentalism, the mid-nineteenth-century American philosophical movement. They trace its roots to Puritan self-reliance and European Romanticism (reacting to the Enlightenment and French Revolution), describe the Transcendental Club and The Dial, and discuss its emphasis on imagination, intuition, and individual connection to the divine. They profile Henry David Thoreau's time at Walden Pond (misconceptions about his isolation), his jailing and tax resistance over the Mexican-American War and slavery that led to "Civil Disobedience," and the movement's activism in education reform, abolition, and women's rights, highlighting Margaret Fuller. They close with the movement's decline and lasting influence, followed by listener mail about chickens in ancient Rome.

entities.name: Handbook to Life in Ancient Rome

segments.title: Opening banter and personal connections to Transcendentalism
segments.summary: Hosts share how they got into Transcendentalism as teens and in college, Josh's trail cam bear sighting, and their mixed feelings about the Transcendentalists before deciding Thoreau deserves an episode.

segments.title: Defining Transcendentalism as a philosophy
segments.summary: Hosts describe the mid-1830s movement's core idea that everyone has divine light and should be self-reliant, and note its association with action as well as writing. They say the movement struggled when trying to ground itself in formal theory.

segments.title: Roots: Puritans and European Romanticism
segments.summary: The Puritans' individualism and direct connection to God influenced Transcendentalist self-reliance. European Romanticism, a reaction to Enlightenment rationalism and the French Revolution, emphasized emotion and imagination; American scholars gained access to it after the Paris Peace Treaty of 1815.

segments.title: The Transcendental Club, The Dial, and imagination over facts
segments.summary: George Ripley founded the Transcendental Club in Boston in the mid-1830s, and the group published The Dial, a literary quarterly-style paper. The hosts explain the movement's preference for imagination over facts and its goal of a better society through individual fulfillment, with a Plato anecdote.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before the Thoreau segment.

segments.title: Thoreau at Walden Pond and misconceptions
segments.summary: Thoreau built a one-room cottage on Emerson's land at Walden Pond. The hosts counter the myth that he lived completely isolated, noting he walked to town, dined with Emerson, and received visits and baked goods from family.

segments.title: Thoreau's tax resistance, jail, and Civil Disobedience
segments.summary: Thoreau refused to pay a poll tax to protest slavery and the Mexican-American War, was jailed for a night, and someone anonymously paid his debt against his wishes. The experience inspired his essay Civil Disobedience, and the hosts read quotes from it.

segments.title: Transcendentalist activism: education and abolition
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the movement's activism, including education reform with free, open schools founded by several Transcendentalists, and abolitionist work including Thoreau as an Underground Railroad conductor.

segments.title: Margaret Fuller and women's rights
segments.summary: Margaret Fuller, a non-religious Transcendentalist and Dial editor, wrote Woman in the Nineteenth Century and led feminist Conversations. She went to Italy during its revolution, then died in a shipwreck near America's shore along with her husband and son.

segments.title: Decline and legacy of Transcendentalism
segments.summary: The movement burned bright and faded by the 1850s, as key figures died young and the scientific method turned attention back to reason. The hosts argue its ideals persist in social and environmental justice and in appreciating nature.

segments.title: Listener mail: chickens in ancient Rome
segments.summary: Listener Mike Traina writes that chickens were rare in ancient Rome, eaten mainly by aristocrats and used for divination by augurs, and recommends the book Handbook to Life in Ancient Rome. The hosts sign off.
